creative.body:
My daughter is a gastroenterologist who specializes in motility disorders.

She told me to stop taking Miralax and start asking why my stomach had stopped emptying.

That was the best medical advice I've ever received.

I know how that sounds. Your own child telling you to question what your doctor prescribed.

But Sarah works with GLP-1 patients every day. And what she told me at my kitchen table that Saturday afternoon was this:

The reason your gut isn't responding to Miralax, fiber, magnesium, or probiotics is that all of those products work six feet downstream from where the actual problem is.

Your medication slowed your stomach. Every product you've been told to buy works on your colon.

That single sentence is the reason I'm writing this.

I'm 67. I started Mounjaro in February. By April the constipation had taken over my life.

Seven days sometimes without a single movement. Bloating so severe I looked pregnant by lunchtime. Sulfur burps mid-conversation I couldn't predict or control. Trapped gas that never let up.

I started keeping a list in my phone of restaurants by how close their bathrooms were to the front door, because I didn't trust my body to make it to the back of the dining room.

If you're on a GLP-1 and any of that sounds familiar, keep reading. Because what my daughter explained to me that afternoon is something almost no doctor is telling women your age, and the reason most women quit these medications inside a year has nothing to do with the medication itself.

It has to do with the wrong organ.

My doctor said the same thing every visit. Normal side effect. Eat more fiber. Take Miralax. Your body will adjust.

I took the fiber. It made my bloating ten times worse.

I did the Miralax cleanout. Entire bottle in Gatorade. Spent the night doubled over, sweating, running to the bathroom every twenty minutes while my husband sat on the edge of the bed asking if I needed to go to the ER.

Two days later the constipation was back like nothing happened.

Probiotics. Nothing. Magnesium citrate. Worked for a week, then stopped. Gas-X. Took the edge off for an hour.

Between the Miralax, the fiber, the probiotics, the magnesium, and a gut health supplement from Amazon, I was spending over $90 a month.

My gut kept getting worse.

I wasn't sleeping. I wasn't eating real meals. I'd cut down to crackers and broth most nights because the pressure of food on top of food on top of food was unbearable.

I was on a weight loss medication and I was starving myself on top of it. Not to lose weight. To avoid the feeling of food sitting inside me for four days.

When my doctor mentioned moving me to a stronger prescription laxative, I called Sarah.

She went quiet on the phone. Then she said, "Mom, can I come over Saturday? I need to walk you through something."

She drove three hours. That's when I knew this wasn't casual.

We sat at my kitchen table. She had her laptop open. My daughter, the one I used to quiz on biology flashcards, was about to give me a medical education my own doctor never did.

"Mom, do you know how many women I see every week who took their Miralax every single day, ate their fiber, did everything right, and still ended up with a gut that completely stopped responding?"

"I don't want to think about that."

"Almost all of them are on a GLP-1."

She turned her laptop toward me.

"Think of your digestive system like a highway. Food enters at the on-ramp, your stomach. It travels through. It exits at the off-ramp, your colon."

Simple enough.

"Mounjaro slows the on-ramp to almost nothing. That's how it works. That's the mechanism that makes you lose weight. Your stomach used to empty in about four hours. On this medication it can take ten or twelve. Food just sits there."

She pulled up a diagram.

"When food sits that long, bacteria ferment it. They produce sulfur gas, methane, hydrogen. The gas expands your stomach wall. That's your bloating. That's the sulfur burps. That's the pressure that never lets up. Your stomach is literally a fermentation tank right now."

I just stared at her.

"Now here's the part that should make you furious. Every product you've been taking. The Miralax, the fiber, the stool softeners, the probiotics. They all work at the off-ramp. They all target the colon. But nothing is backed up in your colon, Mom. The blockage is six feet upstream. In your stomach. You've been treating the exit when the problem is at the entrance."

My chest got tight. I couldn't breathe right for a second.

"Why didn't Dr. Patel tell me this?"

Sarah closed her eyes for a second.

"Because the standard protocol is fiber, Miralax, and stronger prescriptions if those don't work. That's what the guidelines say. It doesn't matter that I work in motility every single day and watch the protocol fail for GLP-1 patients constantly. The protocol is the protocol."

I want you to sit with that for a minute. Because if you're suffering the way I was, this is the part that matters most.

Your doctor is not lying to you. Your doctor is following a protocol that was written before GLP-1 medications existed at the scale they exist now. The protocol assumes the problem is in the colon. It almost never is when you're on this class of drug.

Sarah walked me through every product in my cabinet.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften stool. There was barely any stool in my colon to soften. The food was still trapped in my stomach. So I'd been hydrating an empty pipe.

Dulcolax triggers contractions in the colon wall. There was nothing in my colon to push. So my colon was contracting around empty space. Cramping with zero results.

Magnesium citrate. Same organ. Same wrong organ.

Probiotics seed beneficial bacteria into a section of the gut that wasn't the section that was broken. They were working downstream of the actual problem.

And fiber. Fiber was the cruelest one. Adding bulk to a system where the stomach had already stopped moving forward just made the backup worse. The pressure got worse. The bloating got worse. And nothing came out anyway.

"You weren't failing the protocol, Mom. The protocol was wrong for you. They had you adding food to a stomach that couldn't process the food it was already holding."

If that paragraph hit you the way it hit me, you already understand why nothing has been working for you either.

"So what do I do?"

"You stop treating your colon and start supporting your stomach."

She showed me the research. Three things had to work together.

The first was apigenin. A flavonoid concentrated in celery juice extract. Not celery powder, not celery seed. The extract.

It wakes up the muscles in the stomach wall. A natural prokinetic that promotes the contractions that push food out of the stomach. Works at the on-ramp, where the medication actually caused the slowdown.

"And before you ask, Mom — no, this won't undo Mounjaro. The medication's appetite work is in your brain. The stomach slowing is a side effect that contributes to feeling full, not the engine of it. Apigenin doesn't bring your stomach back to where it was before. It brings it from frozen to slow. The drug keeps doing its job. Food just stops fermenting inside you."

This isn't even a new idea, Sarah said. Twenty-four hundred years ago, Mediterranean women chewed celery stalks before meals to wake up a stalled stomach. Hippocrates wrote about it. We forgot, because we built a pharmaceutical industry around colon-targeted laxatives and never circled back.

The second was chlorophyllin. A stabilized form of chlorophyll that binds directly to the sulfur compounds and methane from the fermentation. It doesn't mask it. It neutralizes it at the molecular level, right where it's happening.

The third was soluble prebiotic fiber. Different from the bulk-forming fiber my doctor kept pushing. This kind feeds beneficial bacteria in the lower gut and produces butyrate, which keeps the colon moving once the stomach starts emptying again. The downstream support, not more bulk packed onto a closed on-ramp.

"Most products on the shelf are colon products, Mom. You need something that works at the on-ramp."

She'd already found one. A small company called Motilli.

Celery juice gummies. Concentrated apigenin. Chlorophyllin. Soluble prebiotic fiber. All three. In a gummy that doesn't depend on the system that's backed up to deliver it.

"It's a gummy on purpose, Mom. A capsule has to dissolve in stomach acid before any of the actives release. Which requires a stomach that's actually working. You're a perfect example of someone for whom a capsule wouldn't reliably do its job. A gummy is essentially pre-dissolved. Releases the actives almost immediately, even on a stalled stomach."

She ordered it for me before she left.

I won't pretend I believed it would work. After eight months and six products, I'd stopped believing in any of it. I just didn't have the energy left to argue with her.

Week one. Nothing.

I texted Sarah that I didn't think it was working. She wrote back, "It's been five days, Mom. Give it time."

Week two. The pressure under my ribs started easing. Not gone. But lighter than it had been in months.

I noticed it in line at the grocery store. I was just standing. Not shifting my weight foot to foot. Like a normal person standing in line.

Week three. I went. On my own. No magnesium the night before. No Miralax. No emergency cleanout. I just woke up and went.

I sat on the edge of the tub afterward and tried to remember the last time my body had done that on its own.

Week four. I pressed my hand into my stomach one morning. Soft. No wincing. I almost didn't trust it.

Month two. Sunday dinner at my son's house. Long table. Too much food. Stayed for coffee afterward. Came home without changing into elastic pants.

Month four. I wasn't planning my day around my gut anymore. I wasn't checking restaurant floor plans. I wasn't skipping dinner to avoid the pressure of food on food on food. I was just living.

And the weight kept coming off the whole time. Sarah had told me it would. The medication was finally being allowed to do its job without dragging my digestion under with it.

Five months after Sarah drove three hours to sit at my kitchen table, I went back to my doctor.

She pulled up my previous notes. Then the new ones.

"Your bowel movements are daily. The bloating has resolved. You're still losing weight. What changed?"

"I stopped treating my colon and started supporting my stomach. Every product you prescribed works at the off-ramp. GLP-1 medication slows the on-ramp. The blockage was six feet upstream from where any of it could help."

She looked at me. Then at the chart. Then back at me.

"I'd like to understand what you're taking."

"I'll have Sarah send you the research."

I want to tell you about my sister Diane.

Diane started Wegovy six months before I started Mounjaro. She quit at month four. The constipation was so bad she said it felt like she'd swallowed a brick that wouldn't pass.

Her doctor told her the same thing mine was telling me. Eat more fiber. Take the Miralax. Drink water.

She quit the medication. Gained every pound back inside a year. She's spent the three years since trying every diet and drug she can find, and none of them touched what the GLP-1 was doing for her.

Diane didn't quit because the medication failed her. She quit because nobody told her the constipation was a stomach problem, not a colon problem. By the time anyone might have, she'd already given up.

That was almost me. It might be you.

If you've been on a GLP-1 for more than a few months and your gut has stopped working, you are roughly where Diane was when she threw her pen in the trash. The path from where you are to quitting is shorter than you think. The fiber makes it worse. The Miralax stops working. The cleanouts get more brutal. Eventually the math of suffering versus weight loss flips.

That whole sequence is preventable. It starts with treating the right organ.

Motilli celery juice gummies. Two a day.

No cleanouts. No fiber feeding the fermentation. No more treating the wrong organ. Just a stomach that empties again, even on the medication.

I was spending over $90 a month on Miralax, fiber gummies, magnesium, probiotics, and a gut supplement from Amazon, all of them working on the wrong organ.

Motilli costs less per day than what I was wasting on a single one of those products. They're running a promotion right now that takes another chunk off, and the link below has the current pricing.

90-day no-questions-asked guarantee. If your digestion isn't measurably better, full refund. Sarah told me about that part before I ordered. She said anyone who's been told for eight months to "just eat more fiber" while suffering every day deserves to find out without risking anything else.

One thing she warned me about. Motilli is a small company. They batch-produce because the apigenin starts to degrade once it's exposed to light and time. That's why most celery extract supplements on the shelf don't work. They sat in a warehouse too long.

Motilli doesn't keep months of inventory. The trade-off is that batches sell out for a few weeks at a time, especially when more women find them. If they're in stock when you click through, that's the day to order.

There are two versions of the next year for you.

In one of them, you keep doing what you're doing. Fiber, Miralax, magnesium, all of it pointed at the wrong organ. Eventually the suffering wins, the way it won with Diane. You quit the medication. You gain the weight back. And next Christmas you're sitting in the same chair watching the grandkids the same way she has been for three years now.

In the other one, you stop treating the wrong organ. The stomach starts emptying. The bloating drops. The bathroom maps come off your phone. You stay on the medication that was working, because the only reason you were going to quit is gone.

That's the whole choice. Stop following the protocol that's failing you. Start supporting the organ that actually needs it.

The link is below if you want it.

P.S. If you have a sister or a friend on a GLP-1 who's been suffering with the same thing, send this to her. The reason Diane gained the weight back wasn't the medication. It was that nobody told her in time. I'm trying to do for someone else what Sarah did for me.
